target.title: fix(agents): add missing return after agent_end case in event dispatcher
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

In `createEmbeddedAgentSessionEventHandler` (`src/agents/embedded-agent-subscribe.handlers.ts:156-159`), the `case "agent_end"` branch calls `scheduleEvent()` but does not `return`. Every other case in the switch (`message_start`, `message_update`, `message_end`, `tool_execution_start`, `tool_execution_end`, `compaction_end`) correctly uses `return`. This means execution falls through to `default:` after handling agent_end.

## Why This Change Was Made

The `default:` case is currently empty, so the bug is latent. However, the missing `return` creates a fragile invariant where any future code added to `default:` would be silently triggered after every agent_end event.

## User Impact

- Before: agent_end handler falls through to default: after execution
- After: agent_end handler returns after execution, consistent with all other event types
- No user-visible impact currently (default is empty), but prevents future control-flow bugs

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior addressed:** Missing return after agent_end case in event dispatcher switch
- **Real environment tested:** Linux x86_64, Node 24, commit `c58f2ee4f` on branch `fix/missing-return-agent-end-handler` (rebased on upstream/main `94e1cc9a4`)

target.title: fix(ai): keep OpenAI tool call id truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`normalizeToolCallId` in `openai-completions.ts:1052` truncates oversized OpenAI tool call IDs with `id.slice(0, 40)`. When a tool call ID contains a UTF-16 surrogate pair straddling positions 39-40, `slice` splits the pair and leaves an unpaired high surrogate — producing **invalid Unicode in the outbound API request**.

## Why This Change Was Made

`String.prototype.slice(0, 40)` operates on UTF-16 code units. A surrogate pair (e.g. 🐱 `\uD83D\uDC31`) consumes 2 code units. The fix switches to `truncateUtf16Safe(id, 40)` from `@openclaw/normalization-core/utf16-slice`, an existing repo helper used by sibling UTF-16 PRs (#104054, #107664, #109561, #109498, #109839).

Sibling surfaces (non-OpenAI provider paths, other `normalizeToolCallId` branches) are unaffected — the change is scoped to the `model.provider === "openai"` check at line 1053.

Collision check: searched open PRs for `normalizeToolCallId`, `truncateUtf16Safe`, `tool_call_id`, `surrogate pair`; no same-file or same-problem open PR was found.

## User Impact

- Multi-model `openai` provider tool-call conversations produce valid Unicode in all IDs
- No change for IDs without surrogate pairs at the 40-unit boundary
- Non-OpenAI provider paths unchanged

## Evidence

Exact head: `72acbae1fefd4416744c8d1491a414e89354fdbc`

`oxfmt --check packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.ts packages/ai/src/providers/openai-completions.test.ts` — passed.

target.title: fix(scripts): bound check-workflows subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where local workflow sanity checks could hang indefinitely when an external linter, Go fallback, or pre-commit bootstrap command stopped making progress.

## Why This Change Was Made

`scripts/check-workflows.mjs` now applies a bounded timeout to each subprocess it launches, escalates non-cooperative children after a short grace period, and reports which command timed out. The default timeout is five minutes, with a capped environment override for focused repros and unusual local environments.

## User Impact

Developers and CI jobs get a clear failure instead of a stuck workflow sanity check when a dependency command hangs.

## Evidence

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/check-workflows.test.ts`
- Real entrypoint proof with an `actionlint` fixture that ignores `SIGTERM`:

```text
$ PATH="$fixture/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs
fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan ignores SIGTERM
status: 1
stderr: [check-workflows] timed out after 500ms: actionlint .github/workflows/android-release.yml ... .github/workflows/workflow-sanity.yml
```

<details>
<summary>proof-check-workflows-timeout.sh</summary>

```sh
#!/bin/sh
set -eu

node_bin="$(command -v node)"
proof_dir="$(mktemp -d)"
mkdir -p "$proof_dir/bin"

cat > "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint" <<SH
#!$node_bin
if (process.argv[2] === "--version") process.exit(0);
process.on("SIGTERM", () => {});
setInterval(() => {}, 10_000);
SH
chmod +x "$proof_dir/bin/actionlint"

set +e
PATH="$proof_dir/bin" OPENCLAW_CHECK_WORKFLOWS_COMMAND_TIMEOUT_MS=500 "$node_bin" scripts/check-workflows.mjs >"$proof_dir/stdout.txt" 2>"$proof_dir/stderr.txt"
exit_code=$?
set -e

printf 'entrypoint: node scripts/check-workflows.mjs\n'
printf 'fixture: actionlint --version succeeds; actionlint workflow scan ignores SIGTERM\n'
printf 'status: %s\n' "$exit_code"
printf 'stderr: %s\n' "$(tr '\n' ' ' < "$proof_dir/stderr.txt" | sed 's/  */ /g')"
```

</details>

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where successful Tlon / Urbit login responses could make `openclaw` drain an arbitrarily large or slowly streaming response body before returning the authentication cookie.

## Why This Change Was Made

The Tlon auth path still performs a best-effort body drain for Urbit setups that finalize cookies after response consumption, but now bounds that compatibility drain by both a 64 KiB byte cap and one short overall drain deadline. Users can still authenticate against normal Urbit responses, while oversized, stalled, or slow-trickling successful login bodies no longer keep the login flow tied to unbounded response consumption.

target.title: fix(config): ignore inherited keys when restoring env refs
target.body:
## Summary

Use `Object.hasOwn(parsed, key)` when restoring environment references so inherited properties are not treated as authored configuration.

## What Problem This Solves

`restoreEnvVarRefs` accepts plain-object values whose prototype may be customized. Its object branch iterates own `incoming` entries, but the previous `key in parsed` check also admitted inherited `parsed` properties. An inherited environment-reference template could therefore replace an incoming own value even though that template was never authored on the parsed object.

## Root Cause

- `in` traverses the prototype chain.
- `Object.hasOwn` matches the authored-key semantics used by adjacent config helpers.
- `isPlainObject` intentionally accepts custom prototypes, so narrowing the membership check is the correct local owner-boundary fix.

## Why This Fix

- One canonical own-property check at the restoration decision.
- No parser normalization, compatibility shim, or broader `isPlainObject` contract change.
- Matches sibling config-path and merge-patch own-key handling.

## User Impact

Normal JSON and JSON5 config behavior is unchanged. Internal or custom callers that pass plain objects with custom prototypes no longer restore inherited environment-reference templates.

## Evidence

- The original submitted test also passed with the old implementation, so the maintainer fixup replaced it.
- The repaired regression creates a custom prototype carrying an inherited template.
- With `key in parsed`, the focused suite fails because the inherited template is restored.
- With `Object.hasOwn`, the incoming value is preserved.

## Tests and Validation

- Blacksmith Testbox baseline: 1 focused regression failure with the old membership check.
- Blacksmith Testbox fixed: `src/config/env-preserve.test.ts` passed, 72/72 tests.
- Targeted `oxfmt --check` passed.
- Maintainer autoreview passed with no findings.
- Exact-head hosted CI is required before merge.

Not required: internal hardening with no documented JSON or JSON5 behavior change.

target.title: fix(agents): avoid synthetic overflow in tool-heavy sessions
target.body:
Closes #107655

Related: #107821

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where long-lived, tool-heavy sessions could discard a provider-acceptable projected prompt and trigger whole-session compaction when conservative local character estimates reported pressure.

On current `main`, a restored session with twelve 50k-character tool results manufactured a local context overflow before provider submission. Recovery compacted and persistently rewrote the session even though the controlled provider accepted the projected prompt.

## Why This Change Was Made

Generic aggregate, preflight, and tool-loop character pressure now remains prompt-shaping and diagnostic input rather than proof of context overflow. Explicit opt-in mid-turn recovery remains unchanged. When a provider actually rejects context, the existing recovery path records the final provider request identity and prevents resending a byte-identical rejected payload while allowing materially changed retries.

This addresses the common false-positive authority across all three generic gates. #107821 is a useful narrow mitigation for successful aggregate replacement, but it leaves the normal preflight estimator and always-on tool-loop character guard able to manufacture the same overflow without a provider rejection.

No configuration, protocol, provider identity, public API, or persisted-session format changes.

AI-assisted: yes. I traced the runtime and upstream Codex contracts, reviewed every accepted autoreview finding, and understand the implementation and proof.

## User Impact

Tool-heavy sessions can submit their bounded provider prompt without premature compaction or history loss. Genuine provider context rejections still use bounded recovery, and an identical rejected request cannot enter a retry loop.

## Evidence

Deterministic Gateway reproduction on the current-main baseline:

- Accumulated twelve real 50k-character `exec` results under a 1.05M model window.
- Restarted the Gateway with the same model set to 272k, then sent a normal follow-up.
- Baseline made 15 provider calls, triggered synthetic compaction, and retained only 1/12 historical tool results.

Exact final patch on Blacksmith Testbox via Crabbox:

- The same real Gateway restart scenario passed in 14 provider calls.
- All 12/12 historical tool results and the newest sentinel reached the follow-up request.
- The follow-up completed without rerunning tools.
- Private reproduction harness remained under ignored `.artifacts/` and is intentionally not part of this PR.

Regression and repository proof:

- Focused prompt projection, admission, overflow, and compaction suite: 394/394 passed across 14 files.
- Fresh Codex autoreview: no accepted/actionable findings.
- `pnpm check:changed` on Testbox: passed, including production/test typechecks and full selected lint/policy gates (13m50s).
- `pnpm build` on Testbox: passed (1m22s).
- `git diff --check`: passed.

target.title: refactor(gateway): simplify lifecycle mutation contracts
target.body:
## Summary

Post-landing cleanup of the gateway lifecycle surface from #110323 / #110497 — scar tissue from the start-stopped-delegating-to-restart evolution, plus contract tightening. No behavior change except one new warning.

- Delete the impossible "scheduled" start outcome: every platform `start()` completes synchronously; the branch and its restart-worded response were fossils. `start()` contracts are now completed-only.
- `GatewayLifecycleMutationMode` union replaces stringly-typed audit modes (29 literals now compile-checked); drop the never-supplied `pid` field; one shared best-effort mutation reporter (`service-mutation.ts`) so observer exceptions can never interrupt service control on any path.
- Already-running start now surfaces previously discarded repair drift as a warning (text + JSON `warnings[]`) instead of silently swallowing it; still strictly idempotent — no repair, no restart.
- Action-specific `ServiceRecoveryResult` types (start recovery can no longer claim "stopped").
- Remove dead launchd handoff `label`/`$5` plumbing.
- Micro-dedup: cached TTY check in `run.ts`; `forceFreePort()` reuses `killPids`.

## Proof

- Focused suites green: daemon 298 passed, CLI 173, recovery/repair neighbors 75 — including `daemon-cli.coverage` and `lifecycle-core.config-guard`.
- `tsgo:core` + `tsgo:test:src` green (Blacksmith Testbox); targeted oxlint clean; max-lines ratchet OK.
- Structured review (Codex gpt-5.6-sol): clean, no actionable findings.

Release-note context: `gateway start` now warns when the already-running service's installed definition has drifted and needs `gateway restart` to apply.

target.title: fix: preserve same-session hook bursts
target.body:
Closes #110109

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users sending multiple `/hooks/agent` events to the same resolved session could lose later events when the first event was still claiming the cron session lifecycle.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agent hook dispatch now uses a per-session FIFO queue inside the already-tracked detached gateway root work. Same-session hook events run in arrival order, while different session keys keep independent queues. Failed hook runs still report their existing system event and do not block the next queued event.

AI-assisted maintainer fix.

## User Impact

Webhook bursts for one target session no longer drop loser events as non-retryable `CronSessionLifecycleClaimError` failures. Operators can keep normal cron concurrency without forcing all hook work through a global single-run bottleneck.

target.title: fix(secrets): surface degradation in logs and doctor
target.body:
Related: #101265

## What Problem This Solves

SecretRef degradation can leave one owner cold at startup or keep a stale last-known-good value after reload, but the primary operator signal was easy to miss and could expose low-level resolution text.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Emits a warning-level structured `secrets.degraded` log at startup and reload with redacted owner kind, owner id, reason, cold/stale state, and the `openclaw secrets reload` retry hint.
- Keeps exact owner isolation: a failed webhook route stays cold while unrelated routes remain available.
- Makes doctor list degraded owners with the same redacted reason and retry guidance.
- Attributes typed reload failures to the actual failed owner; an unmapped typed failure reports conservative `unknown:unmapped` / cold metadata without leaking the SecretRef id.

Per maintainer decision, this PR adds no `secrets.degraded[]` gateway protocol/status field, schema, generated Swift model, protocol version bump, config option, parameter, environment variable, UI, or new capability.

## User Impact

Operators get a loud signal in the existing web UI log view and a human-readable doctor section. Public webhook requests remain generic `401 unauthorized`; secret values and SecretRef ids are not logged.

## Evidence

- Exact rebased head: `7296c6bf718d92ecd069c5f21c965d7489ca6589`
- Focused behavior suite: 185 tests passed across gateway startup, runtime secrets, fast path, web tools, auth integration, state, and doctor.

target.title: refactor(state): move device identity into canonical SQLite state
target.body:
Related: #107227

## What Problem This Solves

OpenClaw still treated `identity/device.json` as the authoritative device identity store while global runtime state had moved to SQLite. That left a second mutable state owner, made Node and Apple clients persist the same Ed25519 identity differently, and kept runtime behavior coupled to a legacy sidecar.

## Why This Change Was Made

This moves the stable device identity keypair into the existing typed `device_identities` table in the shared state database. Runtime code reads and writes SQLite only. `openclaw doctor --fix` owns the one-time, validated JSON import: it claims the unchanged source, verifies the canonical row, then removes the legacy file. Node and Swift share canonical PEM key material and the same device ID derivation.

The change is additive at the database layer: it reuses the already-shipped table and does not advance `user_version`. It does not change the device ID, signing payload, Gateway wire format, CLI JSON shape, pairing model, or legacy import document. Device auth tokens remain a separate migration because their gateway-scoped key requires a different additive table.

## User Impact

Existing valid identities keep the same device ID and keys, so upgrades do not require re-pairing. Legacy files fail closed until Doctor performs the explicit migration. Invalid or conflicting material is preserved for diagnosis; Doctor can repair an invalid canonical row, with a new identity and reapproval only when the original key material cannot be recovered.

This is a one-way database-first cutover. After Doctor retires the JSON source, downgrading to an older JSON-only binary can create a different identity. Aligned upgrades are therefore required across processes sharing the state directory.

## Evidence

- Exact rebased head: `4328e273b565dc0abe0d37c64bbe8e7d9fa91871`; clean merge against current `main`.
- Blacksmith Testbox changed-surface gate passed at that head: type checks, formatting, core and scripts lint, package and plugin boundaries, macOS packaging tests, database-first guards, runtime import-cycle checks, and the remaining classified gates. Run: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29637761945. The backing action can show cancellation after the delegated lease is intentionally stopped; the wrapper completed with exit code 0.
- Focused TypeScript proof: 40 device-identity and Doctor-migration tests, 86 state-database tests, and 488 database-first guard tests passed.
- Focused Swift proof: 91 `DeviceIdentityStoreTests` and `GatewayNodeSessionTests` passed, including Node PEM interoperability, timestamp reconciliation, auth ownership conflicts, profile isolation, strict legacy validation, schema gates, WAL behavior, and gateway session identity use.
- `git diff --check` passed. The rebased branch and the stacked PortGuardian branch both have clean merge trees.
- Fresh autoreview of the final hardening commit found no actionable issue. The whole-branch bundle safety scanner continues to reject synthetic device-key fixtures before model invocation; earlier independent whole-branch migration/race/security and Swift–Node reviews were clean.

## Maintainer Decision Pending

Please explicitly accept or defer the documented one-way cutover: Doctor-required legacy import, coordinated versions for processes sharing one state directory, and no supported downgrade to a JSON-only binary after migration.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound CLI installer smoke fetch
target.body:
AI-assisted: yes (Codex)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the CLI installer non-root Docker smoke could pipe an unbounded installer download directly into bash, allowing a stalled download to hang the smoke step.

## Why This Change Was Made

The smoke now downloads the CLI installer to a temporary file with curl connection and total-transfer deadlines, removes the temporary file on exit, and then runs the same installer arguments.

## User Impact

CLI installer smoke runs now fail within a bounded download window instead of waiting indefinitely before installer execution.

## Evidence

Validated on current head `38102f27036c40114b35c198fe120a7a07b7cb82`.

- Real Docker success path: ran the CLI installer download/execution sequence as the non-root `node` user in `node:22-bookworm` with `OPENCLAW_NO_ONBOARD=1` and `OPENCLAW_NO_PROMPT=1`; observed `OpenClaw installed (OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4))`, `installed_path=/home/node/.openclaw/bin/openclaw`, and `OpenClaw 2026.7.1 (2d2ddc4)`.
- Real Docker forced-failure path: ran the same `curl ... -o "" ... && bash "" --set-npm-prefix --no-onboard` sequence against a container-local response that drops the connection after writing an installer marker; observed `curl_chain_status=52`, `marker=absent`, and `proof-failure-complete`, proving the installer is not executed after a failed download.

target.title: fix(tui): stop Codex login lookup hanging the terminal
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The local TUI resolved the Codex executable synchronously before starting the OpenAI/Codex login flow. A stalled PATH lookup could leave the TUI suspended indefinitely without opening any login UI.

## Why This Change Was Made

Codex CLI discovery now runs through OpenClaw's asynchronous process runner with a five-second hard timeout, bounded output, and `SIGKILL`. It preserves trusted Windows `where.exe` selection and the first PATH match. Timeout, lookup failure, or an empty result returns `null`, preserving fallback to OpenClaw's local provider-auth flow.

## User Impact

Starting Codex authentication from the TUI no longer blocks the event loop or waits forever on a wedged binary lookup. Healthy Codex discovery and the existing fallback remain unchanged.

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox: `pnpm test src/tui/tui.resolve-codex-bin.test.ts src/tui/tui.test.ts` — 2 files, 62 tests passed. Run: https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/actions/runs/29638302322
- Regression coverage includes timeout, successful POSIX first-match selection, trusted Windows `where.exe`, no-match fallback, and the awaiting TUI caller.
- `git diff --check` passed.
- Fresh autoreview of the final branch reported no actionable findings.
- Direct upstream contract check: Codex CLI defines `codex login`; OpenClaw continues delegating only the OpenAI auth path to that command.

Not exercised: a live Windows host or completing an actual Codex OAuth login. Windows command selection is covered by the focused test.
